outcome: No credible mathematical progress on the conjecture itself was found since 26 January 2024. The only candidate event is a July 2025 self-published blog post claiming an AI (Grok 4) produced a disproof; it has no arXiv trace, no author identity findable, no peer review, and no independent discussion anywhere (MathOverflow, Reddit, mathematical blogs, or citation indexes), so it does not meet the bar for counting as a change of status.
summary: The Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture (a group of cohomological dimension 2 has a 2-dimensional K(G,1)) remains listed as open in every standard reference checked, including the current Wikipedia article, which still describes only the 1997 Bestvina–Brady dichotomy (their group is a counterexample to either Eilenberg–Ganea or Whitehead's conjecture, but it is not known which) with no update reflecting any resolution. The one item surfaced by both my search and the triage pass is a July 2025 blog post at zeropoint.sh titled 'Definitive Resolution of the Eilenberg–Ganea Conjecture via Twisted Bredon Cohomology,' which claims that Grok 4 (xAI) produced a complete disproof by showing the Bestvina–Brady group has cohomological dimension 2 but geometric dimension 3, via a non-vanishing twisted Bredon cohomology class. I could not fetch the page directly (WebFetch and Bash curl both failed to reach zeropoint.sh — DNS resolution failure in this sandbox), so I relied on search-engine synthesis of its content and independently verified the surrounding claims: there is no arXiv preprint matching this description (searches for 'Eilenberg-Ganea' combined with 'twisted Bredon cohomology' and 2025/2026 date ranges return only unrelated legitimate papers on Bredon cohomology theory), no author name or institutional affiliation for the blog is discoverable, and no mathematician, forum (MathOverflow), or survey discusses or cites the claim. A claim of this magnitude — resolving a 67-year-old conjecture — receiving zero uptake anywhere in over a year is itself strong evidence against it having survived even cursory scrutiny, though the complete absence of any critique or rebuttal (rather than a documented refutation) also means I cannot rule out that it is simply unknown/unseen rather than checked-and-rejected. Genuinely related 2024 progress exists in adjacent group-cohomology territory (e.g., Kielak–Linton on Baumslag's conjecture, Fournier-Facio–Sun on realizable dimension sets, work on Nucinkis's conjecture) but none of it bears on cd(G)=2 implying gd(G)=2 specifically; these are variants/neighbours under §3.1, not cases of this problem, so they do not change the status. Given no verifiable, expert-digested, or even independently-citable result exists, I classify this as open with no_change_found true. I disagree with the triage's 'possible' verdict only in emphasis, not conclusion: it correctly withheld a status change, and I confirm that after deeper investigation (attempting direct access to the blog, searching for arXiv traces, checking Wikipedia's live article, and checking for community discussion) no evidence changes that conclusion.
competing_reading: If the zeropoint.sh manuscript is in fact a real, correct, technically detailed disproof (its description of exploiting the known Bestvina–Brady dichotomy — resolving Eilenberg–Ganea negatively while leaving Whitehead's conjecture untouched — is at least structurally consistent with the known mathematics, since the dichotomy requires exactly one of the two to fail), then the correct status would be 'claimed' with ai_role 'generated' and resolution_direction 'refuted', dated 2025-07-10. I was unable to read the manuscript itself (only search-engine summaries of the blog page), so I cannot rule out that it contains genuine technical content; I am instead relying on the near-total absence of any independent trace, verification, or discussion as the basis for not counting it.
what_would_settle_it: Direct access to the zeropoint.sh page and any linked manuscript/PDF (currently unreachable from this environment), confirmation of whether it was ever posted to arXiv or a preprint server under a named author, and any response from a topologist or group theorist (e.g., on MathOverflow, a blog, or in a citing paper) either endorsing or refuting the specific twisted Bredon cohomology argument.
